translation: She looks at the family, all girls, a mother with a child at her breast clumsily dismounting from a farm cart while the driver hurries her, because it needs to return for others in the suburbs.
A bundle that she had on her back slips off; some slightly grayed pieces of cloth and a string of tiny, darkened beads spill out.
She collects them embarrassingly as if she has just unveiled her deepest secrets before the world's eyes.
Deymowa walks past her and suddenly a boy around six or seven years old runs up to her.
Looking at her with smiling eyes, very pleased with himself he says: "Praise be to Jesus Christ!".
She automatically but solemnly responds: 'Forever and ever, amen.
But immediately thereafter clutches her heart as tears well up in hers eyes.
She squats next to the boy, grabs his wrists while he meets straight into hers eyes brimming over with tears still wearing an amused smile like little rascals do.
The first buildings loom before them all of a sudden, without warning.
Apparently, the fog changes the sense of distance, as even Kaśka seems surprised by this.
Suddenly she jumps, jerking at the shafts and would've upset the carriage if not for Roszek's decisive reaction and his whip.
Maybe it was the sparks showering from the forge that scared Kaśka, or perhaps it was the nervousness of horses awaiting their turn to be shod.
Everywhere carries the sickly smell of malt, penetrating every product on sale.
One might as well eat it like bread.
In the suburbs of Rohatyn, in Babintsy, there are a few small breweries; that's where this enriching smell engulfs the whole area from.
Many small shops sell beer here and better-stocked establishments have both vodka and mead for sale three-part mead predominantly.
The Jewish merchant Wakszul offers wine true Hungarian and true Rhine wine as well as a slightly sour variety brought all the way from Wallachia.
There would be much to say about the Wolowski family, as it has grown immensely in size.
Nearly all branches of this family were ennobled, some as Bawół coat of arms and others as Na Kaskach.
Undoubtedly Franciszek, son of Isaac Wołowski who Chmielowski referred to as Jeremiah made a great career for himself.
Born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach, he became one of the finest lawyers and experts on law of his time.

Interestingly, when a proposal was introduced to grant Polish citizenship to Jews in parliament, Franciszek then an MP delivered an impassioned speech arguing that it was not yet time for such a step.
Firstly, the Polish nation had to achieve independence before considering social reforms.
All the neophytes from Offenbach were buried in the city cemetery, which after many years began to interfere with city development plans and was eliminated in 1866.
The bones of those buried there were collected and respectfully reburied elsewhere.

On this occasion, the skull of Jakub Frank was exhumed from his grave and meticulously labeled and identified as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch", ended up in hands of the historian for the city Offenbach.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances it made its way to Berlin, where it underwent extensive measurements and studies and was declared an example of Jewish racial inferiority.
After war it vanished without a trace perhaps destroyed by wartime havoc, turned into dust or still lies stored away in underground warehouses of some museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great peace came for me.
My main pursuit became the study of Merkavah, supplemented by our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski since we shared a room, which brought us closer together.
I told Jeruchim about Chai Szor, that she was the only woman I could love and did love from that beautiful moment when I got her for one night when I arrived in Rohatyn with news about Jakub.
But above all else, I loved Jakub.
They had been in Ivany since April.
If it weren't for the kind people of Ivany, they would probably have starved to death.
Ivany saved their lives and health, Bejla is feeling better now and doesn't cough as much.
Srol believes that once they are baptized, they will be as well off as the Christians.
They will get a piece of land, Bejla will have vegetables in her garden and he, Srol, will weave rugs because he can do that well.
In old age when their daughters are married off, they'll move in with them.
These are all his dreams.
"Look, benefactor, Kaśka doesn't want to go," Roszko says grimly when the sleigh stops.
Roszko gets off the seat and waves his hand energetically several times in farewell.
Then he leans over and peers into the fog as if looking into water.
A shirt protrudes from under his festive red, though somewhat faded, coat.
"I don't know where to go," he says.
"What do you mean you don't know?
We're already on the Rohatyn road," says the priest, surprised.
Indeed!
He gets out of the sleigh and follows his servant, circling helplessly around carriage and straining their eyes into white expanse.
They think they see something but their eyes that can't latch onto anything begin playing tricks on them. .
That something like this could happen to them!
It's as if one had lost oneself in one's own pocket.
"Quiet!" suddenly says the priest lifting a finger above him to listen closely. .
And indeed from somewhere on left side through swirls of fog comes a weak sound of rippling water.
"Let's follow this sound.
That's flowing water", decides with determination  ,the  Priest .
Soon the priest relaxes in his cart, stretches out his legs in front of him and lets his eyes wander over the sea of fog.
Immediately he falls into a journeyman's reverie, for thinking is best done on the move.

Slowly, reluctantly, the mechanism of his mind comes alive; gears and cogs engaging to set the drive wheels in motion, just like in the clock that stands in his rectory hallway, bought in Lviv; he paid a considerable amount for it.
In a moment it will chime "bim-bom".
Maybe this world originated from such fog?
He begins to ponder.
After all, Jewish historian Josephus Flavius claims that world was created during autumn equinox.
This could be true given there were fruits present in paradise; if an apple hung from a tree then it must have been fall.
There is some logic to this thought but then another springs into mind:
What kind of argument is that?
Couldn't an almighty God create tiny fruits aboveboard regardless of season?
When they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join a stream of pedestrians, horsemen, and vehicles of all kinds that emerge from the fog like bread dough figurines made for Christmas.
It's Wednesday; market day in Rohatyn.
Farmer's wagons loaded with sacks of grain, cages with poultry, and various farm products are on their way.
Between them briskly march traders carrying every possible item from their stalls on their backs like yokes;
in a moment these will become tables piled high with colorful fabrics, wooden toys, and eggs bought up in villages at a quarter of the price. ..
The peasants also lead goats and cows intended for sale; terrified by the noise, the animals balk at puddles.
A rag-covered cart full of boisterous Jews rushes past them:
drawn to Rohatyn's fair from all over the area‒and then laboring past there is a grand carriage which struggles to maintain its dignity amidst fog and crowd congestion:
its shiny lacquered doors are blackened by mud while driver's face under his blue cloak seems sour;
evidently he did not expect such commotion and is now desperately looking out for an opportunity to get off that damnable road.
